title: The mango simile
hook: a man asleep under a tree, woken by a falling mango, picks it up, smells it, eats it: the steps of one perception (a commentary simile)

segments.voice: Yesterday, a mug crashed in the next room, and the Abhidhamma slowed the moment down: turn, see, sort, respond. Your line: seeing is a process. Did you catch a reaction as its own step? Day one thousand sixty-nine.

Hot afternoon. A man lies asleep at the foot of a mango tree, his head covered with a cloth. The leaves are still. Then a ripe mango lets go of its branch, drops, and lands with a thump right by his ear. That's the whole setup. It isn't from the suttas. It's a simile from the commentaries, the teachers who came after and tried to make the Abhidhamma's road easy to remember. Yesterday's process was a diagram. Today it gets a body, a tree, and a piece of fruit.
screen: `ASLEEP UNDER A MANGO TREE.` → `A THUMP BY HIS EAR.` → `A DIAGRAM GETS A BODY.`

segments.voice: Follow the man, and you're following yesterday's road. First, sleep. His sleep is the quiet current of the mind, running along with nothing in particular in it. The falling mango is the object striking, and the thump that wakes him is the current being cut. Second, he wakes and turns. He pulls the cloth off his head and looks around: the mind turning toward the door the object came in by. He sees the mango: just seeing. Third, the sorting. He reaches out and picks it up: receiving. He squeezes it a little: examining. He smells it, and decides: ripe. That's the settling, the moment that says, this is a mango, a good one. Fourth, the eating. He eats it, and enjoys it. In the simile, the eating is the response, javana, the stage where the mind acts and kamma is made. Then he swallows the last of the taste, lies back down, and falls asleep again. The current runs on, quiet, until the next mango. Notice the order of things he chose and things he didn't. He didn't choose the mango falling. He didn't choose waking. He didn't decide to see it. Most of the simile happens to him. Only at the eating does the man do something, and even then it is a very ordinary thing. That's the point the teachers wanted remembered. Life drops mangoes. Sounds, sights, a message, a smell from someone's kitchen. Most of the road is automatic. The place to look is the eating: what the mind does with what has fallen. And then, the simile says, back to sleep, until the next thump.
screen: `SLEEP, AND A THUMP.` · `HE WAKES, TURNS, SEES.` · `PICKED UP, SQUEEZED, SMELLED.` · then, large: `THE EATING IS WHERE HE ACTS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: eat one fruit very slowly. If you have a piece of fruit nearby, a grape, a slice of apple, a raisin, hold it. If not, use a sip of water or tea. First, just look at it. Then feel its weight and skin. Bring it close and smell it. Notice when the mind says: ripe, good, I want this. Then eat it, slowly, and watch the liking happen. Swallow, and rest. Sit in the quiet after, the way the man lies back down under his tree. The bell holds the time.
The mango simile. A commentary picture of one perception: the man asleep, the falling fruit, waking, seeing, picking up, smelling, eating, and sleep again. Today's word.
Your line: the mango falls. Today, when something drops into your day, a message, a noise, a smell, let it fall, and watch what you do when it's time to eat. Day one thousand sixty-nine.

howItsDone: Teachers of the Abhidhamma in Theravada communities use the mango simile to explain the stages of a single perception, and some insight meditation retreats use slow, mindful eating as an exercise.

options: you climb the tree for more

original.note: Pali: mango, the fruit and the tree.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about a lucky nap.
what it means: a picture of one perception, from the mango striking to the eating, where the mind finally acts.
what a scholar hears: a commentarial simile, found in the Atthasalini, that maps sleep to the life-continuum (bhavanga) and the eating to javana.
